intro: Look across the four landscape studies and note where the light gathers. Each approach makes a different scale of place and weather visible.
alt: Four landscapes show a clouded English field, an American mountain river, a woodland edge and a still river beneath a pale horizon.

variants.name: English landscape painting
variants.look: Thick-moving clouds hang over a relatively close view of paths, fields and hedges.
variants.history: English landscape painting encompasses many approaches. John Constable's early nineteenth-century pictures made familiar rural places and observed weather prominent subjects.
variants.when: Study a particular Constable painting when shape and movement in the sky need to make a place feel lived in.
variants.why: Changing patches of light tie the weather to the land beneath rather than making it a distant background.

variants.name: Hudson River School
variants.look: A distant opening of light pulls the eye up from darker foreground slopes and along the river.
variants.history: Nineteenth-century American painters including Thomas Cole created ambitious landscapes. Their views of land and nature circulated alongside national expansion and its exclusions.
variants.when: Study how layered masses and directional light can convey a vast region in a single view.
variants.why: The changing scale of detail leads viewers from a particular foreground into an immense distance.

variants.name: Barbizon School
variants.look: Soft tree edges, dull greens and opening patches of daylight keep attention near the woodland floor.
variants.history: Nineteenth-century painters associated with Barbizon worked in and around France's Fontainebleau forest and developed attentive approaches to everyday landscape.
variants.when: Study this when a modest scene needs detail and atmosphere without a monumental view.
variants.why: A close viewpoint makes the forms, shade and textures of ordinary ground worth studying.

variants.name: Luminism
variants.look: The long river horizon and smooth bands of reflected light leave the boats tiny against the sky.
variants.history: Luminism is a later label for part of nineteenth-century American painting, commonly associated with clear atmosphere, quiet water and controlled finish.
variants.when: Study it when you want to make subtle light conditions the main subject.
variants.why: Smooth transitions and a steady horizon keep viewers attentive to minute changes in light.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: English landscape painting: stippled fresh summer hedges, big mobile cumulus, rutted path and distant study of farmland; Hudson River School: panoramic romantic American mountain and river, dramatic break of radiant light over deep foreground; Barbizon School: modest woodland edge and patient seated figure painted in browns and soft greens near the ground; Luminism: smooth cool low river horizon and tiny points of boats, pale bands of reflected light and almost invisible strokes. Show repeat character as a tiny modern visitor in artwork alone. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
